before: 204. At the risk that moralizing will show itself here, too, as what it has always been—namely, a determined MONTRER SES PLAIES, in Balzac's phrase—I venture to protest against an unjust and harmful reversal of rank. Almost unnoticed, and apparently with a perfectly clear conscience, this reversal now threatens to establish itself in the relationship between science and philosophy. What I mean is that one must have earned, through one's own EXPERIENCE—and doesn't experience, as I understand it, always mean unhappy experience?—the right to discuss so important a question of rank. Otherwise one talks about colour like a blind man, or talks AGAINST science like women and artists (“Ah! this dreadful science!” their instinct and their shame sigh, “it always FINDS THINGS OUT!”). The scientific man's declaration of independence, his emancipation from philosophy, is one of the subtler consequences of democratic organization and disorganization. Everywhere the scholar's self-glorification and self-importance are now in full bloom, enjoying their finest spring—which is not to suggest that self-praise smells sweet in this instance. Here, too, the instinct of the populace shouts, “Freedom from all masters!” Science resisted theology, whose “hand-maid” it had been for far too long, with the happiest results. Now, in its recklessness and lack of discretion, it proposes to legislate for philosophy and become the “master” in its turn—what am I saying! to act as the PHILOSOPHER on its own authority. My memory—the memory of a scientific man, if you please!—overflows with the innocently insolent remarks about philosophy and philosophers I have heard from young naturalists and elderly doctors. I need hardly mention the most cultivated and conceited of all scholars, philologists and schoolmasters, who are both by profession. Sometimes it was the specialist, the Jack Horner in his corner, instinctively defending himself against every task and ability that brings things together. Sometimes it was the industrious worker, who had detected OTIUM and a refined taste for luxury in the philosopher's inner household, and felt hurt and diminished by them. At other times it was the utilitarian's colour-blindness: he sees in philosophy only a succession of REFUTED systems and an extravagant expense that “does nobody any good”. Sometimes what stood out was fear of concealed mysticism and of efforts to redraw the boundaries of knowledge; sometimes contempt for particular philosophers had inadvertently grown into contempt for philosophy itself. Most often, behind young scholars' proud disdain for philosophy, I found the damaging after-effect of one particular philosopher. They had generally renounced allegiance to him, but had not escaped the spell of his scornful judgments of other philosophers; the result was hostility to philosophy as a whole. (This, for example, seems to me Schopenhauer's effect on the newest Germany. His unintelligent fury against Hegel succeeded in cutting an entire recent generation of Germans off from German culture. Taken as a whole, that culture had raised the HISTORICAL SENSE and refined it into something almost prophetic; yet precisely here Schopenhauer himself was impoverished, unreceptive, and un-German to a positively ingenious degree.) Broadly speaking, perhaps the modern philosophers' own humanity, their all-too-human character—in short, their contemptible qualities—has done the deepest damage to respect for philosophy, throwing the doors open to the instinct of the populace. Just acknowledge how far our modern world has departed from the whole manner of Heraclitus, Plato, Empedocles, and all those other royal, magnificent hermits of the spirit, whatever their names. Acknowledge, too, how justly an honest man of science MAY feel himself better born and bred when he looks at the representatives of philosophy whom current fashion places as high as they actually stand low: in Germany, for instance, those two Berlin lions, the anarchist Eugen Duhring and the amalgamist Eduard von Hartmann. Above all, the spectacle of these patchwork philosophers who call themselves “realists” or “positivists” is calculated to plant a dangerous distrust in an ambitious young scholar's soul. At best these philosophers are themselves only scholars and specialists: that much is plain! They have all been defeated and BROUGHT BACK AGAIN under the rule of science. At some point they demanded more of themselves, without having a right to that “more” or to the responsibility it involves. Now, with conviction, resentment, and a desire for revenge, their words and actions express DISBELIEF in philosophy's ruling task and supremacy. After all, how could things be otherwise? Science flourishes today, its clear conscience written openly on its face. Meanwhile the condition to which the whole of modern philosophy has gradually declined, the little that remains of philosophy today, provokes distrust and displeasure, if not contempt and pity. Philosophy reduced to a “theory of knowledge”, little more in fact than a timid science of periods and a doctrine of restraint; philosophy that never gets past the threshold and sternly DENIES itself permission to enter—that is philosophy in its death throes, an ending, an agony, something to arouse pity. How could philosophy of that kind—RULE!

before: 205. Today the philosopher faces so many dangers in his development that one might doubt whether this fruit can still ripen at all. The sciences have expanded enormously in breadth and in the height of their structure. With that expansion grows the likelihood that the philosopher will become exhausted while still a learner, or settle somewhere and “specialize”, never reaching his own height: his superspection, circumspection, and DESPECTION—the vantage from which he can look above, around, and down. Or he reaches that height too late, after the best of his maturity and strength has gone, or when he has been damaged, coarsened, and worn down, so that his view, his overall judgment of things, no longer counts for much. Perhaps it is precisely the delicacy of his intellectual conscience that makes him hesitate and linger along the way. He fears becoming a dilettante, a millepede, a milleantenna—a creature with a thousand feet and a thousand antennae. He knows only too well that a discerning man who has lost his self-respect can no longer command, no longer LEAD—unless he intends to become a grand actor, a philosophical Cagliostro and spiritual rat-catcher: in short, someone who leads people astray. In the last resort this is a question of taste, unless it has really been a question of conscience all along. To double the philosopher's difficulties once more, he also demands a verdict from himself, a Yes or No, about life and life's value rather than about science. Reluctantly he learns to believe that obtaining this verdict is his right, even his duty. He must find his way to that right and that belief through the widest range of experiences, perhaps experiences that unsettle and destroy him, often hesitating, doubting, and struck dumb. He feels the obligation and the burden of a hundred trials and temptations in life; he continually stakes HIMSELF, and plays THIS bad game.

before: 206. Beside a genius—a being who either ENGENDERS or PRODUCES, both words taken in their fullest sense—the learned man, the average scientific man, always has something of the old maid about him. Like her, he has no practical acquaintance with humanity's two principal functions. Naturally we grant respectability to both scholar and old maid, almost as compensation—in these cases we lay particular stress on respectability—and yet our obligation to make this concession carries the same touch of irritation in each case. Let us look more closely: what is the scientific man? First, an ordinary sort of person with ordinary virtues: a type who neither rules nor speaks with authority nor stands independently. He is hardworking, patiently adaptable to his place in the ranks, even-tempered and moderate in both abilities and demands. He has an instinct for people of his own kind and for what they need: for example, their patch of independence and green meadow, without which there is no rest from work; their claim to honour and consideration, which above all requires being recognized and recognizable; the sunshine of a good reputation; and the constant confirmation of their value and usefulness. Such confirmation must repeatedly overcome the inner DISTRUST rooted in the hearts of all dependent people and herd animals. As one would expect, the learned man also has ailments and faults of an ignoble sort. Petty envy fills him, and he has a lynx's eye for weaknesses in people whose heights he cannot reach. He is trusting, but only like someone who lets himself go without ever beginning to FLOW. Precisely before a man who is a mighty current, he grows colder and more guarded; his eye becomes a still, unresponsive lake, no longer stirred by enthusiasm or fellow-feeling. The worst and most dangerous thing a scholar can do springs from his type's instinct for mediocrity, from the Jesuitism of mediocrity. This instinctively works to destroy exceptional people and tries to break—or, better still, slacken—every drawn bow. Slacken it, of course, with consideration, and naturally with a gentle hand: to RELAX it through trusting sympathy is the true art of Jesuitism, which has always known how to present itself as the religion of sympathy.

before: 207. However gratefully we welcome the OBJECTIVE spirit—and who hasn't grown sick to death of subjectivity and its damned IPSISIMOSITY!—we must eventually learn to be cautious even about our gratitude. We must put an end to the extravagant celebration of the spirit's loss of self and personality, as though this were an end in itself, salvation and transfiguration. Such celebrations are especially customary among pessimists, who in their turn have good reasons for heaping the highest honours on “disinterested knowledge”. The objective man no longer curses and complains like the pessimist. He is the IDEAL scholar, in whom the scientific instinct at last flowers fully after a thousand total or partial failures. Certainly he is among the most precious instruments in existence, but he belongs in the hands of someone more powerful. He is only an instrument, we might say, a MIRROR—not a “purpose in himself”. In truth the objective man is a mirror trained to bow down before everything that wants to be known. His only desires are those involved in knowing or “reflecting”. He waits for something to arrive, then sensitively opens himself to it, so that even the lightest footsteps and the gliding passage of spiritual beings leave their trace on his surface and film. Whatever “personality” he still has seems accidental to him, arbitrary, or more often a disturbance: so thoroughly has he learned to regard himself as a channel and reflection for external forms and events. Remembering “himself” costs him an effort, and he often gets it wrong. He readily confuses himself with other people and misunderstands his own needs; in this one matter he is insensitive and careless. Perhaps he worries about his health, or about the pettiness and narrow atmosphere of his wife and friend, or about lacking companions and society. He actually sets out to think about his suffering, but in vain! Already his thoughts wander towards the MORE GENERAL case, and tomorrow he will know no better than yesterday how to help himself. He no longer takes himself seriously or gives himself time. He is serene, NOT because he has no troubles, but because he cannot grasp and attend to HIS troubles. His habitual readiness to accommodate every object and experience, the radiant, impartial hospitality with which he welcomes everything coming his way, his thoughtless good nature and dangerous indifference between Yes and No: alas! there are plenty of occasions when he must pay for these virtues! As a human being in general, he becomes all too easily the CAPUT MORTUUM of such virtues. Ask him for love or hatred—love and hatred as God, woman, and animal understand them—and he will do and supply what he can. But don't be surprised if it amounts to little, if precisely here he proves false, fragile, dubious, and diminished. His love is forced; his hatred is manufactured, a kind of UN TOUR DE FORCE, a little display and exaggeration. He is genuine only insofar as he can be objective; only in his serene completeness does he remain “nature” and “natural”. His soul, forever reflecting and polishing itself, no longer knows how to affirm or deny. He issues no commands and destroys nothing. “JE NE MEPRISE PRESQUE RIEN”, he says with Leibniz: let us neither overlook nor underestimate that PRESQUE! Nor is he an exemplary man. He leads no one and follows no one; generally he stands too far away to have any reason to take the side of good or evil. If he has so long been confused with the PHILOSOPHER, with the Caesarian educator and dictator of civilization, he has received far too much honour. What matters more in him has been missed: he is an instrument, something like a slave, certainly the most exalted kind of slave, but nothing in himself—PRESQUE RIEN! The objective man is an instrument, an expensive measuring and reflecting apparatus, easily damaged and tarnished, to be cared for and respected. But he is no goal, no movement outward or upward, no completing human being in whom the REST of existence finds its justification, no ending—and still less a beginning, a begetting or first cause. He is nothing tough, powerful, centred in himself, and eager to rule. He is more like a soft, swollen, delicate, movable potter's form, waiting for some content and framework to which it can “shape” itself: usually a man without framework or content, a “selfless” man. Consequently he is also no use to women, IN PARENTHESI.

before: 208. When a philosopher today announces that he is no skeptic—I hope the preceding description of the objective spirit has made that clear?—everyone listens impatiently. This admission makes people somewhat afraid of him; they would like to ask so very many questions... Indeed, timid listeners, who are so numerous now, henceforth call him dangerous. His rejection of skepticism seems to let them hear a distant, threatening noise, as though somebody somewhere were testing a new explosive, a dynamite of the spirit, perhaps a newly discovered Russian NIHILINE, a pessimism BONAE VOLUNTATIS. Such pessimism does not merely deny and intend denial, but—terrible thought!—PUTS denial INTO PRACTICE. Against this kind of “good-will”, a will to the actual, effective negation of life, everyone nowadays acknowledges that no sleeping draught or sedative works better than skepticism: the gentle, agreeable, soothing poppy of skepticism. Today's doctors even prescribe Hamlet as an antidote to the “spirit” and its underground rumblings. “Aren't our ears already full of evil noises?” the skeptics ask, loving their peace and acting almost as a sort of security police. “This underground No is dreadful! Quiet, you pessimistic moles!” The skeptic really is a delicate creature, frightened far too easily. His conscience has been trained to jump at every No, and even at a sharp, decisive Yes, as though something had bitten him. Yes! and No!—both seem to him contrary to morality. Instead he likes to celebrate his virtue through a noble detachment, perhaps saying with Montaigne, “What do I know?” Or with Socrates, “I know that I know nothing.” Or, “Here I don't trust myself; no door stands open for me.” Or, “Even if the door were open, why should I go straight in?” Or, “What good are hasty hypotheses? Perhaps making no hypotheses at all would show perfectly good taste. Must you immediately straighten everything crooked, plug every hole with some sort of oakum? Isn't there time enough for that? Doesn't time itself have leisure? Oh, you demons, can't you WAIT at all? Uncertainty has its charms too; the Sphinx is also a Circe, and Circe was also a philosopher.”—That is how a skeptic consoles himself, and he does indeed need consolation. For skepticism is the most spiritual expression of a particular, many-sided physiological constitution, usually called nervous weakness and sickliness. It develops whenever races or classes long kept apart suddenly and decisively mix. The new generation has inherited, as it were in its blood, different standards and valuations; everything in it is unrest, disorder, doubt, and tentative experiment. Its best powers check one another, its very virtues prevent one another from growing strong. Body and soul lack balance, ballast, and upright stability. But what is most diseased and degenerate in these mixed beings is the WILL. They no longer know independent decision or the brave pleasure of willing; even in their dreams they doubt “freedom of the will”. Present-day Europe is the scene of a senseless, hurried attempt to mix classes radically, and CONSEQUENTLY races as well. It is therefore skeptical from its highest levels to its lowest. Sometimes its skepticism is restless, hopping impatiently and recklessly from branch to branch; sometimes it looks gloomy, like a cloud loaded with question marks—and often it is sick to death in its will! Paralysis of the will: where today do we fail to find this cripple sitting! And how dressed up it often is, how seductively decorated! The finest festive clothes and disguises are available for this disease. For instance, most of what now appears in the display windows as “objectiveness”, “the scientific spirit”, “L'ART POUR L'ART”, and “pure voluntary knowledge” is merely skepticism and paralysis of will in costume. I am prepared to stand behind this diagnosis of Europe's illness. The disease of the will is unevenly spread across Europe. It is worst and most varied where civilization has ruled longest; it diminishes wherever “the barbarian” still—or once again—asserts his claims beneath the loose garments of Western culture. Thus, as one can readily establish and understand, the will is weakest in today's France. France has always possessed a masterly gift for turning even the ominous crises of its spirit into something charming and seductive. Now it emphatically demonstrates its intellectual ascendancy over Europe by serving as the school and exhibition of all skepticism's charms. The capacity to will, and to hold to a decision, is already somewhat stronger in Germany; within Germany it is stronger in the North than in the centre. It is considerably stronger in England, Spain, and Corsica, associated with a sluggish temperament in the first and with hard heads in the latter two. I leave aside Italy, still too young to know what it wants, which must first show whether it can exercise a will at all. But the strongest and most astonishing instance is the immense middle empire where Europe seems to flow back into Asia: Russia. There the strength to will has long been stored and accumulated; there the will, uncertain whether to affirm or deny, waits menacingly for its discharge, to borrow our physicists' favourite expression. Perhaps freeing Europe from its greatest danger would require more than wars in India and complications in Asia: perhaps internal upheaval would also be needed, the empire shattered into little states, and above all the introduction of parliamentary stupidity, together with everyone's obligation to read a newspaper over breakfast. I say this without wishing it to happen. At heart I would prefer the opposite: Russia becoming so much more threatening that Europe would have to resolve to become equally threatening itself. That would mean ACQUIRING ONE WILL through a new caste ruling the Continent, a lasting, dreadful will of its own, capable of setting goals thousands of years ahead. Then the endlessly prolonged comedy of its petty states and its many wills, dynastic as well as democratic, could finally end. The age of petty politics is over; the next century will bring the battle for world dominion—the COMPULSION towards great politics.

before: 209. How far the new warlike age, into which we Europeans have plainly entered, might encourage another, stronger kind of skepticism is something I want to discuss for now only through a parable. Lovers of German history will already understand it. That unscrupulous enthusiast for tall, handsome grenadiers, the troubling, half-crazy father of Frederick the Great, had on one point a genius's instinctive knack and lucky grasp. As King of Prussia he brought into being a military and skeptical genius—and with him, in reality, the new German type that has now emerged triumphantly. He knew what Germany then lacked, something whose absence was a hundred times more alarming and serious than any shortage of culture or social polish. His hostility towards young Frederick sprang from the anxiety of a deep instinct. MEN WERE LACKING, and to his bitter sorrow he suspected that his own son was not man enough. On this point he was wrong; but who in his position would not have been wrong? He saw his son slipping into atheism, ESPRIT, and the agreeable frivolity of clever Frenchmen. Behind them he saw that great bloodsucker, the spider of skepticism. He suspected the incurable misery of a heart no longer hard enough for either good or evil, and of a broken will that could no longer command, was no longer ABLE to command. Yet within his son a new, harder, more dangerous skepticism was growing. Who knows TO WHAT EXTENT his father's hatred and the icy sadness of a will sentenced to solitude actually fostered it? This was the skepticism of daring manliness, closely allied to a genius for war and conquest, which first entered Germany in the person of the great Frederick. It despises yet grasps; it undermines and takes possession; it disbelieves without thereby losing itself. It grants the spirit a dangerous freedom while keeping the heart under strict guard. This is skepticism in its GERMAN form: a continuing Fredericianism raised to the highest spiritual level. For a considerable time it has held Europe under the rule of the German spirit and its critical, historical distrust. The extraordinarily strong, tough masculinity of the great German philologists and historical critics gradually established a NEW conception of the German spirit, despite all the Romanticism in music and philosophy. Properly understood, those men were also all artists of destruction and dissolution. In this new conception, the tendency towards masculine skepticism was unmistakable: a fearless gaze, a dissecting hand both courageous and severe, a determined will to undertake dangerous voyages of discovery, spiritual North Pole expeditions beneath barren, perilous skies. Warm-blooded, superficial humanitarians may have good reasons for crossing themselves before this spirit, this CET ESPRIT FATALISTE, IRONIQUE, MEPHISTOPHELIQUE, as Michelet calls it with a shudder. But to grasp how revealing this fear of the “man” in the German spirit is—the spirit that woke Europe from its “dogmatic slumber”—we should recall the older conception that the new one had to overcome. It was not so long ago that a masculinized woman could presume, with complete abandon, to recommend the Germans to Europe's attention as gentle, good-hearted, weak-willed, poetic fools. Finally, we need only understand Napoleon's astonishment on seeing Goethe deeply enough: it reveals what people had meant by “the German spirit” for centuries. “VOILA UN HOMME!”—in other words, “But this is a MAN! I only expected to see a German!”

before: 211. I insist that people finally stop confusing philosophical workers, and scientific men generally, with philosophers. Precisely here we must strictly give “each his own”, rather than give the former far too much and the latter far too little. The genuine philosopher's education may require him to have stood on every step where his servants, the scientific workers of philosophy, stay standing and MUST stay standing. Perhaps he himself must once have been a critic, a dogmatist, a historian, and also a poet, collector, traveller, solver of riddles, moralist, seer, “free spirit”, and almost everything else. Only so can he travel through the whole range of human values and judgments, and BE ABLE, with different eyes and consciences, to look from a height into every distance, from a depth towards every height, from a corner across every open expanse. But these are only preparations for his task. The task itself demands something different: he must CREATE VALUES. Philosophical workers, following the excellent examples of Kant and Hegel, have to establish and formulate some great existing body of valuations. These are earlier DETERMINATIONS OF VALUE, creations of value that have gained acceptance and are called “truths” for a time, whether in the LOGICAL, POLITICAL (moral), or ARTISTIC sphere. Such investigators must make everything that has happened and been valued so far visible, conceivable, intelligible, and manageable. They must shorten everything long, even “time” itself, and SUBJUGATE the entire past. This enormous, wonderful task can surely satisfy every refined pride and every persistent will engaged in carrying it out. GENUINE PHILOSOPHERS, HOWEVER, COMMAND AND LEGISLATE. They declare, “This is how it SHALL be!” They first determine humanity's destination and purpose, and in doing so put aside the previous work of all philosophical workers and all who have subjugated the past. Their creative hand reaches towards the future; everything that exists or has existed becomes their means, their instrument, their hammer. Their “knowing” is CREATING; their creating lays down laws; their will to truth is—WILL TO POWER. Do such philosophers exist today? Have they ever existed? MUST they not exist one day? ...

before: 213. Learning what a philosopher is presents a difficulty: it cannot be taught. One must “know” it through experience—or possess the pride NOT to know it. Nowadays everyone talks about things they CANNOT have experienced; unfortunately this is especially true of talk about philosophers and philosophical matters. Very few know these things, very few are permitted to know them, and every popular notion about them is false. Take, for example, the genuinely philosophical union of bold, overflowing spirituality moving at a presto pace with dialectical rigour and necessity that never makes a false step. Most thinkers and scholars have no personal experience of this union; consequently, if someone describes it in their presence, they find it unbelievable. Every necessity seems to them a nuisance, a painful compulsory obedience, a condition of constraint. They regard thinking itself as something slow and hesitant, almost a burden, and often as “worthy of the SWEAT of the noble”—certainly not as something easy and divine, closely allied to dancing and exuberance! For them “thinking” and approaching something “seriously”, “laboriously”, are one and the same; that is all their “experience” has taught them. Artists may have a finer intuition here. They know very well that precisely when they cease doing anything “arbitrarily” and everything follows necessity, their sense of freedom, subtlety, and power reaches its height: their sense of creatively determining, arranging, and shaping. In short, necessity and “freedom of will” then become the same thing for them. Finally, states of the soul have an order of rank, and problems have a corresponding order. The highest problems ruthlessly repel anyone who ventures too close without being destined to solve them by the height and power of his spirituality. What good does it do when agile everyday minds, or clumsy, honest mechanics and empiricists, push up close to these problems in their plebeian ambition, almost into this “holy of holies”—as happens so often today! Coarse feet must never step on such carpets: the fundamental law of things ensures that. Those doors stay closed to intruders, however often they batter and break their heads against them. One must always be born to a high station, or, more precisely, BRED for it. A person has a right to philosophy, in the higher sense of the word, only through descent; here too ancestors and “blood” decide. Many generations must prepare the way for a philosopher's arrival. Each of his virtues must separately have been acquired, cultivated, passed down, and embodied. This includes not only the bold, easy, delicate movement and flow of his thoughts, but above all readiness for great responsibilities; the majesty of a ruling gaze and a look of contempt; the feeling of distance from the multitude and its duties and virtues; kindly protection and defence of whatever is misunderstood and slandered, whether God or devil; delight and practice in the highest justice; the art of command; breadth of will; the lingering eye that seldom admires, seldom looks upward, seldom loves....

before: 214. OUR virtues? We probably still have virtues of our own, though naturally they are not those solid, sincere virtues for which we respect our grandfathers and also keep them at a little distance. We Europeans of the day after tomorrow, we first arrivals of the twentieth century—with our dangerous curiosity, our many-sidedness and skill at disguise, our mellow, apparently sweetened cruelty of sense and spirit—will presumably, IF we must have virtues, possess only those that have reached an understanding with our most secret, heartfelt inclinations and our most passionate needs. Very well, let us search for them in our labyrinths! We know how many things lose their way there, how many disappear completely! And what could be finer than SEARCHING for one's own virtues? Isn't that almost BELIEVING in one's own virtues? But this “belief in one's own virtues”—isn't it practically the same as what used to be called one's “good conscience”, that long, respectable pigtail of an idea our grandfathers wore behind their heads, and often enough behind their understanding too? So, however little we think ourselves old-fashioned and grandfatherly respectable in other ways, in one respect we remain our grandfathers' worthy grandchildren. We last Europeans with good consciences still wear their pigtail.—Ah! If only you knew how soon, how very soon, things will change!

before: 220. Now that praising the “disinterested person” has become so fashionable, we must discover—probably at some risk—WHAT people actually find interesting. What things generally concern ordinary people deeply and fundamentally, including the cultivated, even the learned, and perhaps philosophers too, unless appearances deceive us? This inquiry reveals that most of what interests and enchants higher natures and more refined, demanding tastes seems entirely “uninteresting” to the average person. If he nevertheless notices devotion to such interests, he calls it desinteresse and wonders how anyone can act “disinterestedly”. Some philosophers have given this popular amazement a seductive, mystical expression pointing beyond this world—perhaps because they had no experience of the higher nature themselves? They might instead have stated the bare, honestly reasonable truth: “disinterested” action is extremely interesting and “interested” action, provided that... “And love?”—What! Must even acting for love's sake be “unegoistic”? You fools—! “And the praise of self-sacrifice?”—Anyone who has really sacrificed something knows that he wanted and received something in return. Perhaps he exchanged something in himself for something else in himself, giving something up here to gain more there, perhaps to be more altogether, or even to feel “more”. But a more fastidious spirit dislikes lingering in this territory of questions and answers. Here truth must suppress so many yawns whenever she is forced to answer. And truth, after all, is a woman: one must not use force on her.

before: 224. The historical sense is the ability to divine quickly the order of rank among the valuations by which a people, community, or individual has lived. It is a “divining instinct” for the relationships between these valuations, and between their authority and that of the forces at work. This historical sense, which we Europeans claim as our special gift, came to us in the wake of the enchanting, mad semi-barbarism into which Europe's democratic mixing of classes and races plunged it. Only the nineteenth century recognized this faculty as its sixth sense. Through that mixture, the past of every form and manner of life, of cultures once closely adjoining and layered over one another, pours into us “modern souls”. Our instincts now reach backward in every direction; we ourselves are a kind of chaos. In the end, as I have said, the spirit discovers its advantage in this. Our semi-barbarism of body and desire gives us secret access everywhere, access no noble age ever possessed. Above all it admits us to the labyrinth of unfinished civilizations and to every kind of semi-barbarism that has existed on earth. Since by far the greater part of human civilization so far has itself been semi-barbarism, the “historical sense” amounts almost to a sense and instinct for everything, a taste and tongue for everything. This immediately shows it to be an IGNOBLE sense. For instance, we enjoy Homer again. Perhaps our happiest acquisition is knowing how to appreciate Homer, whom people of distinguished culture could not and cannot so easily make their own, and scarcely permitted themselves to enjoy. Think of seventeenth-century Frenchmen such as Saint-Evremond, who reproached him for his ESPRIT VASTE, or even Voltaire, that century's last echo. Their palate's decisive Yes and No, their ready disgust, their hesitant reluctance towards anything unfamiliar, their horror of the bad taste even of lively curiosity, and the general unwillingness of every distinguished, self-sufficient culture to admit a new desire, dissatisfaction with its own condition, or admiration for something strange—all this prejudices them even against the world's finest things if those things are not their property or cannot become their prey. No faculty is less intelligible to such people than this historical sense with its servile, plebeian curiosity. Shakespeare presents the same case: that marvellous Spanish-Moorish-Saxon synthesis of taste would have made an ancient Athenian from AEschylus' circle half die of laughter or annoyance. Yet we welcome precisely this wild mixture of colours, this blending of the most delicate, coarse, and artificial, with secret trust and warmth. We enjoy it as an artistic refinement reserved especially for us. We let the repulsive fumes and the closeness of the English populace, in which Shakespeare's art and taste live, trouble us as little as they might on the Chiaja in Naples. There, with every sense awake, we willingly walk on enchanted, despite the smell of drains from the town's lower quarters. We people of the “historical sense” undeniably have our virtues: we are unassuming, unselfish, modest, brave, accustomed to self-control and self-denial, very grateful, patient, and accommodating. Yet for all this we perhaps have little “taste”. Let us finally admit what we find hardest to grasp, feel, taste, and love, what meets our deepest prejudice and almost our hostility: precisely the perfection and final ripeness of every culture and art. It is the essentially noble in works and people, their moment of calm seas and serene self-sufficiency, the golden quality and coolness of everything that has perfected itself. Perhaps our great virtue, the historical sense, necessarily conflicts with GOOD taste, at least with the very bad taste. We can summon up within ourselves only imperfectly, hesitantly, and by force those small, brief, happy gifts and glorifications of human life that shine here and there. I mean those marvellous moments and experiences when a great power voluntarily stops before the limitless and infinite, when an overflowing refined delight is enjoyed through a sudden halt and hardening, through standing firm and planting oneself on still-trembling ground. Let us confess that PROPORTION is foreign to us. What really itches in us is a craving for the infinite, the immeasurable. Like a rider on a horse panting to press forward, we modern people, we semi-barbarians, drop the reins before the infinite. OUR greatest bliss comes only when we—ARE IN THE GREATEST DANGER.

before: 228. I hope I may be forgiven for discovering that all moral philosophy so far has been tedious and belongs among the aids to sleep. In my view, NOTHING has harmed “virtue” MORE than the TEDIOUSNESS of its advocates. Nevertheless, I would not overlook their general usefulness. It is desirable that as few people as possible should think about morals, and consequently highly desirable that morals should never become interesting! But we needn't worry! Things today remain as they always were. I see nobody in Europe who has, or REVEALS, any idea that philosophizing about morals could be dangerous, tricky, and ensnaring, that it could involve DISASTER. Look, for example, at those tireless, unavoidable English utilitarians: how ponderously and respectably they stalk along—a Homeric image would express it better—in Bentham's footsteps, just as he had stalked after the respectable Helvetius! No, Helvetius was no dangerous man, that CE SENATEUR POCOCURANTE, to borrow Galiani's phrase. There is no new thought, no finer turn or better expression of an old thought, not even a proper history of earlier thinking on the subject. Taken altogether, it is an IMPOSSIBLE literature unless one knows how to season it with mischief. The old English vice called CANT, or MORAL TARTUFFISM, has in fact crept into these moralists too, this time disguised as the scientific spirit. If one MUST read them, one must certainly keep an eye on their motives. Nor do they lack a secret struggle with pangs of conscience, which descendants of Puritans must naturally suffer throughout their scientific tinkering with morals. Isn't a moralist the opposite of a Puritan, after all: a thinker who regards morality as questionable, worthy of interrogation, in short as a problem? Isn't moralizing immoral? Ultimately they all want English morality accepted as authoritative because this would best serve humanity, or “general utility”, or “the happiness of the greatest number”—no! the happiness of ENGLAND. By every means they want to persuade themselves that pursuing English happiness—COMFORT and FASHION, and at the highest level a seat in Parliament—is also the true path of virtue. Indeed, they would have it that all virtue the world has known consisted precisely in that pursuit. None of these ponderous, conscience-stricken herd animals, who advocate egoism as a means to general welfare, wants to know or even suspect that “general welfare” is no ideal, goal, or comprehensible concept, but merely a nostrum. What is fair to one MAY NOT be fair to another; demanding one morality for everyone actually harms higher people. In short, there are DIFFERENCES OF RANK between people, and therefore between moralities. These English utilitarians are an unassuming, fundamentally mediocre breed, and, as I said, insofar as they bore us, their usefulness cannot be valued too highly. We should even ENCOURAGE them, as these verses partly attempt: Hail, you worthy barrow-wheelers, Ever “longer—better” dealers, Stiffer still in head and knee; Never thrilled and never jesting, Mediocrity unending, SANS GENIE ET SANS ESPRIT!

before: 229. These later ages may pride themselves on their humanity, but they retain so much fear, so much SUPERSTITION born of fear, of the “cruel wild beast” whose conquest is their particular boast, that even obvious truths have long gone unspoken, as if centuries had agreed to silence them. Such truths seem to help revive the beast supposedly killed at last. Perhaps I take a risk by letting one escape. Let others catch it again and feed it enough “milk of pious sentiment” [FOOTNOTE: An expression from Schiller's William Tell, Act IV, Scene 3.] to make it lie quietly, forgotten, in its old corner. We must learn about cruelty afresh and open our eyes; we must finally learn impatience, so that such shameless, gross errors as ancient and modern philosophers have fostered about tragedy can no longer parade around virtuously and boldly. Almost everything we call “higher culture” rests on making CRUELTY more spiritual and more intense: that is my thesis. The “wild beast” has not been killed at all; it lives and flourishes, and has merely been transfigured. Cruelty constitutes tragedy's painful pleasure. Whatever pleases us in so-called tragic sympathy, and underlies everything sublime, right up to the highest and most delicate thrills of metaphysics, draws its sweetness solely from the cruelty mixed into it. Think of the Roman in the arena, the Christian in the ecstasies of the cross, the Spaniard watching the fire and stake or a bullfight, today's Japanese spectator pushing his way into a tragedy, the worker in the Paris suburbs yearning for bloody revolutions, the Wagnerienne whose will comes unhinged as she “undergoes” “Tristan and Isolde”. What they all enjoy, what they strive with mysterious passion to drink in, is the love-potion of that great Circe, “cruelty”. Here we must entirely set aside the blundering psychology of earlier times, which could teach only that cruelty originated in seeing OTHERS suffer. There is abundant, overflowing enjoyment in one's own suffering too, and in making oneself suffer. Wherever people have been persuaded to deny themselves in the RELIGIOUS sense, or to mutilate themselves, like the Phoenicians and ascetics, or more generally to strip away sensuality and flesh and practise contrition, Puritan spasms of repentance, vivisection of conscience, or Pascal-like SACRIFIZIA DELL' INTELLETO, cruelty secretly entices and drives them onward. It is the dangerous thrill of cruelty TOWARDS THEMSELVES. Finally, consider that even the seeker of knowledge acts as an artist and glorifier of cruelty, compelling his spirit to perceive AGAINST its own inclination and often against his heart's wishes. He forces it to say No where he would like to affirm, love, and adore. Indeed, every profound, fundamental examination of something violates and deliberately injures the spirit's fundamental will, which instinctively seeks appearances and surfaces. Even every desire for knowledge contains a drop of cruelty.

before: 230. Perhaps my reference to a “fundamental will of the spirit” needs more detail to be understood; allow me a word of explanation. That commanding something popularly called “the spirit” wants to rule both inside and outside itself, and to feel that it rules. It has the will to make simplicity from multiplicity, a binding, taming, commanding will, essentially a will to rule. Its needs and abilities here are the same as those physiologists attribute to everything that lives, grows, and reproduces. The spirit's power to appropriate what is foreign shows itself in a strong tendency to assimilate the new to the old, simplify the manifold, and overlook or reject outright contradictions. In the same way, it arbitrarily underlines, emphasizes, and falsifies particular features and outlines in foreign material, in every piece of the “outside world”. Its aim is to incorporate new “experiences”, to fit new things into old arrangements: in short, growth—or, more precisely, the FEELING of growth, the feeling of increased power. The same will employs an apparently opposite impulse: a sudden preference for ignorance, an arbitrary exclusion, the shutting of windows, an inner refusal of this or that, a prohibition on approach. It takes a defensive attitude towards much that could be known, content with darkness and a confining horizon, accepting and approving ignorance. All this is necessary according to the degree of its power to appropriate, its “digestive power”, metaphorically speaking. In fact, “the spirit” resembles a stomach more than anything else. Here too belongs its occasional inclination to let itself be deceived, perhaps with a sly suspicion that things are NOT as they appear but are merely being allowed to pass that way. It delights in uncertainty and ambiguity, rejoices in arbitrary, eccentric narrowness and mystery, in what is too close, in the foreground, in enlargement, reduction, distortion, and beautification. It enjoys the arbitrariness of all these displays of power. Finally, there is the spirit's conscientious readiness to deceive other spirits and put on a show before them: the constant pressure and striving of a creative, shaping, changeable power. The spirit enjoys its cunning and its many disguises, and the security they give it. Precisely its Protean arts protect and conceal it best! AGAINST this inclination towards appearances, simplification, disguise, covering—in short, towards an outside, since every outside is a covering—works the sublime tendency of the seeker of knowledge. He takes things deeply, from many sides, thoroughly, and INSISTS on doing so. This is a kind of cruelty in intellectual conscience and taste, which every courageous thinker will acknowledge in himself, provided he has, as he should, spent enough time sharpening and hardening his eye for self-examination, and is accustomed to severe discipline and even severe words. He will say, “There is something cruel in the direction my spirit takes.” Let the virtuous and kindly try to convince him otherwise! Admittedly it would sound more agreeable if people spoke, whispered, and sang praises of our “extravagant honesty” instead of our cruelty—we free, VERY free spirits. Perhaps THAT will indeed become our posthumous glory one day! Meanwhile, since there is plenty of time until then, we should be the last to dress ourselves in this flowery, fringed moral language. All our previous work has made us sick of that taste and its lively extravagance. They are lovely, glittering, jingling, festive words: honesty, love of truth, love of wisdom, sacrifice for knowledge, the truthful person's heroism. Something in them swells the heart with pride. Yet we hermits and marmots long ago convinced ourselves, in all the secrecy of a hermit's conscience, that this worthy verbal parade also belongs among the old false decorations, frippery, and gold dust of unconscious human vanity. Beneath these flattering colours and fresh paint, the terrible original text HOMO NATURA must again be recognized. In practice, we must translate humanity back into nature; master all the vain, visionary interpretations and subsidiary meanings scratched and daubed over the eternal original text, HOMO NATURA; and ensure that human beings henceforth face human beings as, hardened by scientific discipline, they now face nature's OTHER forms. With fearless Oedipus-eyes and stopped Ulysses-ears, they must be deaf to the lures of the old metaphysical bird-catchers who have piped far too long, “You are more! You are higher! Your origin is different!” This may be a strange, foolish task, but who can deny that it is a TASK! Why did we choose this foolish task? Or, to ask it differently, “Why knowledge at all?” Everyone will ask us this. Pressed in this way, we who have asked ourselves the question a hundred times have found, and can find, no better answer....

before: 231. Learning changes us. As physiologists know, it does what all nourishment does when it does more than merely “preserve”. before: 240. I HEARD Richard Wagner's overture to the Mastersinger again, as though for the first time. It is a magnificent, sumptuous, heavy work of late art, proud enough to assume that two centuries of music remain alive in its listeners if they are to understand it. It honours the Germans that this pride was justified! What flavours and powers, what seasons and climates mingle here! At one moment it strikes us as ancient, at another as foreign, bitter, and too modern. It is as wilful as it is grandly traditional, often mischievous, more often rough and coarse. It has fire and courage, yet also the loose, brownish skin of fruit that ripens too late. It flows broadly and fully; suddenly an inexplicable hesitation appears, like a gap opening between cause and effect, an oppressive dreaminess, almost a nightmare. Already, though, the old stream of pleasure widens again, pleasure in its many forms, old and new happiness. ESPECIALLY present is the artist's delight in himself, which he refuses to hide: his astonished, happy awareness of mastering the devices he uses here, the new, newly acquired, incompletely tested artistic devices he seems to reveal to us. Yet taken altogether there is no beauty, no South, none of the delicate clarity of southern skies, no grace, no dance, scarcely any desire for logic. There is even a certain clumsiness, deliberately emphasized, as if the artist were saying, “It is part of my intention”. Heavy drapery, something wilfully barbaric and ceremonial, a fluttering of learned, venerable conceits and jokes: something German in the word's best and worst senses, something in the German manner, many-sided, shapeless, inexhaustible. A certain German strength and overflowing fullness of soul is unafraid to conceal itself beneath the RAFFINEMENTS of decadence, and perhaps feels most at home there. It is a true, genuine sign of the German soul, simultaneously young and old, overripe yet still too rich in possibilities for the future. This music best expresses what I think of the Germans: they belong to the day before yesterday and the day after tomorrow—THEY HAVE NO TODAY YET.

before: 241. We “good Europeans” also have hours when we allow ourselves warm-hearted patriotism, a plunge back into old loves and narrow views—I have just supplied an example. We have hours of national excitement, patriotic anguish, and every other old-fashioned flood of feeling. Indeed, I can imagine sluggish, hesitant races that, even in our fast-moving Europe, would need half a century to overcome such ancestral attacks of patriotism and attachment to the soil, and return to reason—that is, to “good Europeanism”. But what does that matter today! This is the age of the masses: they prostrate themselves before everything massive. The same holds in politicis. They call a statesman ‘great’ if he builds them a new Tower of Babel, some monstrous empire and power. What do they care that we more cautious, conservative people still hold the old belief that only a great thought makes an action or undertaking great? Suppose a statesman forced his people henceforth to practise ‘high politics’, for which nature had poorly equipped and prepared them, so that they had to sacrifice their old, dependable virtues for the love of a new and doubtful mediocrity. Suppose he condemned his people to ‘practise politics’ altogether, when they had previously had better things to do and think about, and had never been able to shake off, deep in their souls, a sensible disgust at the restlessness, emptiness, and noisy quarrels of essentially political nations. Suppose he stirred his people's sleeping passions and greed, made their former reserve and love of standing apart into a disgrace, their exotic character and hidden persistence into an offence, disparaged their deepest inclinations, overturned their consciences, narrowed their minds, and made their tastes ‘national’—what! A statesman who did all this, for which his people would have to do penance throughout their future, if they had a future, would be GREAT, would he?” “Certainly!” the other old patriot answered fiercely. “Otherwise he COULD NOT have done it! Perhaps wanting such a thing was madness! But perhaps everything great began in just that kind of madness!” “Abuse of language!” his companion shouted back. “Strong! Strong! Strong and mad! NOT great!” The old men had plainly grown heated, shouting their “truths” into each other's faces. Happy and apart, I reflected on how soon someone stronger might master the strong, and on the compensation for one nation's intellectual shallowness: the deepening of another.

before: 242. Whether we call what now distinguishes the European “civilization”, “humanization”, or “progress”, or simply use the political formula of Europe's DEMOCRATIC movement without praise or blame, an immense PHYSIOLOGICAL PROCESS goes on behind the moral and political foreground these formulas indicate. Europeans increasingly grow alike; they increasingly detach themselves from the climatic and hereditary conditions in which unified races arise; they increasingly become independent of any particular environment that would impose the same demands on body and soul for centuries. In other words, an essentially SUPER-NATIONAL, nomadic human type slowly emerges, whose typical distinction, physiologically speaking, is the highest degree of skill and power in adaptation. Great setbacks may slow the TEMPO of this process of the EUROPEAN'S EVOLUTION, yet perhaps they will only increase its force and depth. The still-raging storm of “national feeling” belongs among these, as does the anarchism now appearing. This process will probably produce results its naive promoters and enthusiasts, the apostles of “modern ideas”, would least like to anticipate. The new conditions that, on average, level human beings into mediocrity—useful, industrious, clever herd people capable of many services—are also extraordinarily suited to producing exceptional people with the most dangerous and attractive qualities. Adaptability, daily testing changing circumstances and beginning new work with every generation, almost every decade, prevents the type from becoming POWERFUL. The collective impression of these future Europeans will probably be of numerous, talkative, weak-willed, very handy workers who NEED a master and commander as they need their daily bread. before: 244. Germans were once commonly singled out as “deep”. But now the most successful type of new Germanism hungers for quite different honours, perhaps finding everything deep deficient in “smartness”. Above all, that soul is multiple, varied in origin, piled up and layered rather than actually built: its ancestry accounts for this. A German bold enough to declare, “Two souls, alas, live in my breast”, would guess the truth badly—or, more precisely, fall far short of the true number of souls. The Germans are a people formed from an extraordinary mixing and mingling of races, perhaps even predominantly pre-Aryan; they are the “people of the centre” in every sense. Consequently they are more elusive, expansive, contradictory, unknown, incalculable, surprising, and even frightening to themselves than other peoples are. Certainly neither the “Wars of Independence” nor the French Revolution made him look up with greater joy. The event that led him to RECONSTRUCT his “Faust”, and indeed the whole problem of “man”, was Napoleon's appearance. In some remarks Goethe condemns what Germans pride themselves on with impatient severity, as though speaking from abroad. He once defined the famous German cast of mind as “Indulgence towards its own and others' weaknesses”. Was he wrong? One characteristic of Germans is that people are seldom entirely wrong about them. The German soul contains passages, galleries, caves, hiding places, and dungeons. Its disorder has much of mystery's charm; the German knows the side roads to chaos well. Since everything loves its symbol, he loves clouds and everything obscure, developing, twilight-like, damp, and veiled. Whatever is uncertain, unfinished, shifting, and growing seems “deep” to him. The German himself does not EXIST: he is BECOMING, he is “developing himself”. Hence “development” is the specifically German discovery and success among philosophical formulas, a ruling idea that, together with German beer and music, works to Germanize all Europe. Foreigners are astonished and attracted by the riddles posed by the contradictory character at the German soul's base—riddles Hegel systematized and Richard Wagner finally set to music. “Good-natured and spiteful”: this combination, absurd for any other people, is unfortunately justified all too often in Germany. One need only live among Swabians for a while to know it! The German scholar's clumsiness and social unpleasantness fit alarmingly well with his physical tightrope-dancing and nimble daring, which all the gods have learned to fear. Anyone wanting the “German soul” demonstrated ad oculos need only look at German taste, arts, and manners: what boorish indifference to “taste”! How the noblest and commonest sit side by side! How disordered and rich this soul's whole constitution is! The German DRAGS his soul along; he drags everything he experiences. He digests events badly and never gets “finished” with them. German depth often amounts merely to difficult, hesitant “digestion”. Just as all chronic invalids and dyspeptics like convenience, the German loves “frankness” and “honesty”: being frank and honest is so CONVENIENT! This trustfulness, accommodation, and laying of cards on the table, this German HONESTY, is probably the most dangerous and successful disguise the German now knows. It is his particular Mephistophelean art; with it he can “still achieve much”! The German lets himself go and gazes out with faithful, blue, empty German eyes—and other countries immediately mistake him for his dressing gown! What I meant was this: whatever “German depth” may be, and perhaps among ourselves we take the liberty of laughing at it, we would do well to keep honouring its appearance and reputation. We should not trade our old reputation as a profound people too cheaply for Prussian “smartness” and Berlin wit and sand. It is wise for a people to pose, and LET itself be taken, as deep, clumsy, good-natured, honest, and foolish. Doing so might even be—profound! Finally, let us honour our name: we are not called the “TIUSCHE VOLK”, the deceptive people, for nothing....

before: 245. The “good old” age is gone; it sang itself to an end in Mozart. How fortunate WE are that his ROCOCO still speaks to us, that his “good company”, tender enthusiasm, childlike pleasure in Chinese things and their flourishes, courtesy of heart, longing for elegance, love, light steps and tears, and faith in the South can still appeal to SOMETHING REMAINING in us! Ah, one day that too will be over! But who doubts that understanding and taste for Beethoven will disappear even sooner! He was only the last echo of a break and transition in style, NOT, like Mozart, the final echo of a great European taste that had lasted for centuries. Beethoven stands between an old, mellow soul continually breaking down and a future soul, too young, always COMING. His music is covered by the twilight of eternal loss and eternal extravagant hope, the same light that bathed Europe when it dreamed with Rousseau, danced around the Revolution's Tree of Liberty, and finally almost fell down worshipping Napoleon. But how quickly THIS very feeling now fades, how hard it is today even to GRASP it. How strange to our ears is the language of Rousseau, Schiller, Shelley, and Byron, in whom TOGETHER the same European destiny could SPEAK that knew how to SING in Beethoven! All the German music that followed belongs to Romanticism, a movement historically shorter, more fleeting, and more superficial than that great interlude: Europe's transition from Rousseau to Napoleon and the rise of democracy. Weber—but what do WE care today about “Freischutz” and “Oberon”! Or Marschner's “Hans Heiling” and “Vampyre”! Or even Wagner's “Tannhauser”! This music is extinct, though not yet forgotten. Moreover, Romantic music as a whole was neither noble nor musical enough to hold its place anywhere except in the theatre and before the masses. From the beginning it was second-rate music, little esteemed by genuine musicians. Felix Mendelssohn was different, that serene master whose lighter, purer, happier soul won admiration quickly and was forgotten just as quickly: the beautiful EPISODE of German music. But Robert Schumann took things seriously and was taken seriously from the start; he was the last to establish a school. Don't we now feel satisfaction, relief, deliverance, that this very Romanticism of Schumann's has been overcome? Schumann fled into his soul's “Saxon Switzerland”, with a nature half like Werther and half like Jean Paul—certainly not like Beethoven! Certainly not like Byron! His MANFRED music is a mistake and misunderstanding amounting to an injustice. His taste was fundamentally PETTY: a dangerous inclination, doubly dangerous among Germans, towards quiet lyricism and intoxication with feelings. Always withdrawing, timidly retreating into seclusion, this noble weakling revelled only in anonymous joy and sorrow. A sort of girl and NOLI ME TANGERE from the beginning, Schumann was already merely a GERMAN event in music, no longer a European event as Beethoven had been and Mozart still more so. With Schumann, German music faced its greatest danger: LOSING ITS VOICE FOR EUROPE'S SOUL and sinking into a merely national concern.

before: 251. When a people suffers, and WANTS to suffer, from national nervous fever and political ambition, we must accept that clouds and disturbances will pass over its spirit—in short, little attacks of stupidity. Today's Germans, for example, alternate between anti-French folly, anti-Semitic folly, anti-Polish folly, Christian-romantic folly, Wagnerian folly, Teutonic folly, Prussian folly—just look at those poor historians, the Sybels and Treitschkes, with their tightly bandaged heads—and whatever other names these little darkenings of German spirit and conscience go by. Forgive me if I too failed to escape the disease completely during a brief, daring visit to heavily infected ground. Like everyone else, I began thinking about matters that did not concern me, the first symptom of political infection. About the Jews, for instance, listen to this. I have never yet met a German favourably disposed towards the Jews. However firmly all prudent, politically minded men reject actual anti-Semitism, perhaps their prudence and policy oppose only the feeling's dangerous excess, especially its distasteful, disgraceful expression, rather than the feeling itself. We must not deceive ourselves here. Germany has more than ENOUGH Jews; the German stomach, German blood, finds it difficult, and will long find it difficult, to deal with even this quantity of “Jew”, as Italians, Frenchmen, and Englishmen have done through stronger digestion. That is the unmistakable statement and language of a general instinct which must be heard and acted upon. “Let no more Jews enter! Close the doors, especially to the East, Austria included!” Thus commands the instinct of a people whose nature remains weak and uncertain, easily erased or extinguished by a stronger race. The Jews, however, are unquestionably the strongest, toughest, and purest race now living in Europe. They know how to succeed even under the worst conditions, indeed better than under favourable ones, through virtues of a sort people today would like to label vices. Above all, they possess a firm faith with no need to feel ashamed before “modern ideas”. WHEN they change at all, they change as the Russian Empire makes its conquests: like an empire with plenty of time, not born yesterday, following the principle “as slowly as possible”! A thinker concerned for Europe's future will count on the Jews, as on the Russians, in every view of that future, as the most reliable and probable factors in the great interplay and battle of forces. What Europe now calls a “nation” is really more RES FACTA than NATA, sometimes confusingly close to RES FICTA ET PICTA. In every case it is something developing, young, easily shifted, not yet a race, much less a race AERE PERENNUS like the Jews. Such “nations” should most carefully avoid hot-headed rivalry and hostility! Certainly the Jews COULD now gain ascendancy, indeed literal supremacy, over Europe if they wanted it, or were driven to it, as the anti-Semites seem to wish. It is equally certain that they are NOT working or planning towards that end. Instead, they now wish and desire, even somewhat insistently, to be taken into and absorbed by Europe. They long finally to settle somewhere, accepted and respected, ending nomadic life and the “wandering Jew”. We should certainly acknowledge this impulse and tendency and MEET IT HALFWAY; perhaps it signals a moderation of Jewish instincts. For that purpose it might be useful and fair to banish the anti-Semitic loudmouths from the country. We should make these approaches prudently and selectively, much as the English nobility does. Naturally, the stronger, more sharply defined types of new Germanism could enter relations with the Jews with least hesitation: for example, aristocratic officers from the Prussian border. It would be interesting in many ways to see whether a genius for money and patience, and especially some intellect and intellectuality, sadly lacking there, could be added and cultivated alongside the hereditary art of commanding and obeying, both of which already give that region a classic reputation. But here I should interrupt my festive speech and lively Teutonomania, for I have reached my SERIOUS SUBJECT: the “European problem” as I understand it, breeding a new ruling caste for Europe.

before: 252. The English are no philosophical race. Bacon represents an ATTACK on the philosophical spirit generally; Hobbes, Hume, and Locke represent a lowering and devaluation of the idea of a “philosopher” lasting more than a century. Kant rose up and raised himself AGAINST Hume; Schelling RIGHTLY said of Locke, “JE MEPRISE LOCKE”. Those two hostile brother-geniuses of philosophy pushed in different directions towards opposite poles of German thought, wronging each other as only brothers can. What England lacks and has always lacked was well known to Carlyle, that half-actor and rhetorician, that absurd muddlehead. His passionate grimaces tried to conceal what he knew about himself: what Carlyle LACKED—real intellectual POWER, real DEPTH of understanding, in short, philosophy. Such an unphilosophical race characteristically clings to Christianity: it NEEDS Christianity's discipline to “moralize” and humanize it. The Englishman is gloomier, more sensual, headstrong, and brutal than the German; precisely as the baser of the two, he is also the more pious. His NEED for Christianity is that much GREATER. To sensitive nostrils, English Christianity itself still carries a distinctively English smell of spleen and alcoholic excess, against which it is, for good reasons, used as an antidote: the finer poison neutralizing the coarser. For coarse-mannered people, a finer poisoning really is progress, a step towards spirituality. Christian pantomime, prayer, and psalm-singing still disguise English coarseness and rustic primness most satisfactorily—or, more accurately, explain and express them differently. As for the herd of drunkards and rakes who once learned moral grunting under Methodism, and more recently as the “Salvation Army”, a fit of repentance may indeed be the relatively highest expression of “humanity” to which they can rise. We may reasonably concede that much. Yet even the most humane Englishman offends by his lack of music, figuratively and literally. His body's and soul's movements possess neither rhythm nor dance, not even a desire for rhythm, dance, “music”. Listen to his speech; watch the most beautiful Englishwoman WALKING—nowhere on earth are there lovelier doves and swans—and finally listen to them sing! But I ask too much...

before: 253. Some truths are best recognized by mediocre minds, being best suited to them; some truths have charm and seductive power only for mediocre spirits. We are driven to this probably unwelcome conclusion as respectable but mediocre Englishmen—Darwin, John Stuart Mill, and Herbert Spencer come to mind—begin to dominate the middle-class region of European taste. Indeed, who could doubt that it is useful for SUCH minds to prevail for a time? It would be mistaken to think highly developed, independently soaring minds especially suited to establishing and collecting many small, ordinary facts and drawing conclusions from them. As exceptions, they stand from the outset at something of a disadvantage towards those who are “the rules”. After all, they have more to do than perceive: they must BE something new, MEAN something new, REPRESENT new values! The gap between knowledge and ability may be larger, and more mysterious, than we suppose. The capable person on the grand scale, the creator, may have to be ignorant. Scientific discoveries like Darwin's, on the other hand, may benefit from a certain narrowness, dryness, and hardworking carefulness—in short, something English. Finally, remember that the English, with their profound mediocrity, once before brought about a general decline in European intelligence. What people call “modern ideas”, “the ideas of the eighteenth century”, or “French ideas”—against which the GERMAN spirit rose in profound disgust—is indisputably English in origin. The French merely aped and acted out these ideas; they were their best soldiers and, alas! their first and deepest VICTIMS. Through the devilish Anglomania of “modern ideas”, the AME FRANCAIS has finally grown so thin and wasted that we now recall its sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, its deep, passionate strength and outstanding inventiveness, almost in disbelief. Yet we must firmly uphold this historically just verdict against present prejudices and appearances: European NOBLESSE, in feeling, taste, and manners, in every elevated meaning of the word, is FRANCE'S work and invention. We are driven to this probably unwelcome conclusion as respectable but mediocre Englishmen—Darwin, John Stuart Mill, and Herbert Spencer come to mind—begin to dominate the middle region of European taste. Indeed, who could doubt that it is useful for SUCH minds to prevail for a time? It would be mistaken to think highly developed, independently soaring minds especially suited to establishing and collecting many small, ordinary facts and drawing conclusions from them. As exceptions, they stand from the outset at something of a disadvantage towards those who are “the rules”. After all, they have more to do than perceive: they must BE something new, MEAN something new, REPRESENT new values! The gap between knowledge and ability may be larger, and more mysterious, than we suppose. The capable person on the grand scale, the creator, may have to be ignorant. Scientific discoveries like Darwin's, on the other hand, may benefit from a certain narrowness, dryness, and hardworking carefulness—in short, something English. Finally, remember that the English, with their profound mediocrity, once before brought about a general decline in European intelligence. What people call “modern ideas”, “the ideas of the eighteenth century”, or “French ideas”—against which the GERMAN spirit rose in profound disgust—is indisputably English in origin. The French merely aped and acted out these ideas; they were their best soldiers and, alas! their first and deepest VICTIMS. Through the devilish Anglomania of “modern ideas”, the ÂME FRANÇAISE has finally grown so thin and wasted that we now recall its sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, its deep, passionate strength and outstanding inventiveness, almost in disbelief. Yet we must firmly uphold this historically just verdict against present prejudices and appearances: European NOBLESSE, in feeling, taste, and manners, in every elevated meaning of the word, is FRANCE'S work and invention. European ignobility, the plebeianism of modern ideas, is ENGLAND'S work and invention.

before: 254. Even today France remains the home of Europe's most intellectual, refined culture, its advanced school of taste. But one must know how to find this “France of taste”. Those who belong to it stay well hidden. Perhaps only a few embody and sustain it, and perhaps they do not stand on very strong legs: some are fatalists, hypochondriacs, invalids; others overindulged, overrefined people whose AMBITION is to conceal themselves. All share one trait: they close their ears to the democratic BOURGEOIS's delirious folly and noisy outpourings. For a stupefied, brutalized France now sprawls in the foreground. At Victor Hugo's funeral it recently celebrated a genuine orgy of bad taste and self-admiration. These hidden people share something else: a desire to resist intellectual Germanization—and an even greater inability to do so! In this intellectual France, also a pessimistic France, Schopenhauer has perhaps become more at home and more native than he ever was in Germany. Not to mention Heinrich Heine, long since reincarnated in Paris's more refined and demanding lyric poets; or Hegel, who now exercises an almost tyrannical influence in the form of Taine, the FOREMOST living historian. As for Richard Wagner, the more French music learns to adapt to the actual needs of the AME MODERNE, the more it will “Wagnerite”. We can safely predict that: it is already happening enough! Nevertheless, despite every willing or unwilling Germanization and vulgarization of taste, the French can still proudly claim three things as their inheritance and possession, indelible signs of their old intellectual superiority in Europe. FIRST, their capacity for artistic feeling and devotion to “form”, for which L'ART POUR L'ART and many other expressions were invented. France has possessed this capacity for three centuries. Its respect for the “small number” has repeatedly made possible a kind of chamber music of literature, sought in vain elsewhere in Europe. SECOND, the French can claim superiority through their old, many-sided MORALISTIC culture. Thanks to it, even minor newspaper ROMANCIERS and random BOULEVARDIERS DE PARIS generally display a psychological sensitivity and curiosity of which Germany, for example, has no conception, let alone the thing itself! Germans lack a couple of centuries of the necessary moralistic work which, as I said, France has willingly undertaken. Calling Germans “naive” on that account praises a deficiency. Set against German inexperience and innocence IN VOLUPTATE PSYCHOLOGICA, which is not unconnected with the tedium of German company, stands Henri Beyle. He is the most successful expression of genuine French curiosity and inventiveness in this realm of delicate thrills: that remarkable man who anticipated and ran ahead, traversing HIS Europe with a Napoleonic TEMPO, surveying and discovering, in effect, several centuries of the European soul. It took two generations to CATCH UP with him in one way or another, to divine long afterwards some of the riddles that troubled and enchanted this strange Epicurean and questioner, France's last great psychologist. There is a THIRD claim to superiority: French character successfully combines North and South halfway between them. This makes the French understand many things and imposes other things on them that an Englishman can never comprehend. Their temperament turns alternately towards and away from the South, with Provencal and Ligurian blood occasionally bubbling over. It protects them from the dreadful northern grey-on-grey, from sunless spectral abstractions and impoverished blood, that GERMAN sickness of taste. Its current prevalence has prompted the firm prescription of blood and iron, meaning “high politics”, according to a dangerous healing art that makes me wait and wait, but not yet hope. France also retains an instinctive understanding and ready welcome for rarer, seldom-satisfied people too comprehensive to find contentment in any patriotism. They know how to love the South in the North and the North in the South: born Midlanders, “good Europeans”. BIZET made music for them, this latest genius who saw a new beauty and seduction, who discovered a piece of the SOUTH IN MUSIC.
