before: 256. The nationalistic craze has caused, and still causes, a sickly estrangement among Europe's nations. Shortsighted, hasty politicians now hold power with its help, never suspecting how necessarily temporary their policy of disintegration must be. Because of all this, and much else that cannot presently be mentioned, people now overlook the clearest signs that EUROPE WANTS TO BE ONE, or wilfully misinterpret them. Among this century's deeper, broader-minded men, the true general direction of their souls' mysterious work was to prepare that new SYNTHESIS and tentatively anticipate the future European. Only in their poses, or their weaker moments, perhaps in old age, did they belong to the “fatherlands”. When they became “patriots”, they were merely resting from themselves. I mean such men as Napoleon, Goethe, Beethoven, Stendhal, Heinrich Heine, and Schopenhauer. Do not take it amiss if I include Richard Wagner. We must not let his own misunderstandings deceive us about him—geniuses like him seldom have the right to understand themselves—still less the unseemly noise of present French resistance and opposition to him. The fact remains that Richard Wagner and the LATER FRENCH ROMANTICISM of the forties are intimately, closely related. Their kinship is fundamental, in every height and depth of their demands. In their varied, tumultuous art, it is Europe, ONE Europe, whose soul urgently and longingly presses outward and upward—where? Into a new light? Towards a new sun? But who would try to state precisely what all these masters of new languages could not express distinctly? Certainly the same storm and stress tormented them; these last great seekers SOUGHT in the same way! All were steeped in literature up to their eyes and ears, the first artists of universal literary culture. Most were themselves writers and poets, mediators and mixers of arts and senses: Wagner as musician belongs among painters, as poet among musicians, as artist generally among actors. All were fanatics for EXPRESSION “at any cost”—I especially name Delacroix, Wagner's closest relative. All made great discoveries in the sublime, and also in the disgusting and terrifying; greater still were their discoveries in effect, display, and the art of the show-shop. Their talent exceeded even their genius; they were VIRTUOSI through and through, with mysterious access to everything that seduces, attracts, compels, and overturns. Born enemies of logic and the straight line, they craved the strange, exotic, monstrous, crooked, and contradictory. As people, they were Tantaluses of the will, plebeian upstarts who knew themselves incapable of a noble TEMPO or LENTO in life and action—think of Balzac, for instance. Unrestrained workers, they nearly destroyed themselves through work; rebels against laws and conventions of conduct, ambitious and insatiable, without balance or enjoyment. All finally shattered and sank before the Christian cross, with reason and justice: which of them was deep and original enough for an ANTI-CHRISTIAN philosophy? Taken together, they were a boldly daring, magnificently overbearing class of higher men, soaring and dragging others upward, who first had to teach their century—and it was the century of the MASSES—the concept “higher man”... Let Richard Wagner's German friends discuss whether anything in his art is purely German, or whether its distinction lies precisely in sources and impulses BEYOND GERMANY. In this connection, do not underestimate how indispensable Paris was to the development of his type. At the decisive moment, the force of his instincts made him long to visit it; the entire style of his activity, of his self-appointed apostolate, could perfect itself only in sight of the French socialist original. A subtler comparison may find, to the credit of Wagner's German nature, that he acted in everything with greater strength, daring, severity, and elevation than a nineteenth-century Frenchman could have done, because we Germans are still closer to barbarism than the French. Perhaps Wagner's most remarkable creation is inaccessible, incomprehensible, and inimitable to the entire late Latin race, not just now but forever: Siegfried, that VERY FREE man, probably far too free, hard, cheerful, healthy, and ANTI-CATHOLIC for the taste of old, mellow civilizations. This anti-Latin Siegfried may even have sinned against Romanticism. Well, Wagner amply atoned for that sin in his sad old age. Anticipating a taste that has since entered politics, he began, with his characteristic religious fervour, at least to preach THE ROAD TO ROME, if not to walk it. To prevent misunderstanding of those last words, I call on a few forceful rhymes. They will reveal even to less sensitive ears what I mean, what I mean AGAINST the “last Wagner” and his Parsifal music: Is this our way? From German hearts, this tortured wailing? From German flesh, this self-assailing? These priestly hands spread wide in prayer, This incense rising through the air? This faltering, falling, stumbling motion, This wavering ding-dong of devotion? These sly looks at nuns, these Ave bells ringing, This utterly false, ecstatic heavenward springing? Is this our way? Think hard! You still await admission: What you hear is ROME—ROME'S FAITH BY INTUITION!

before: 257. Every elevation of the type "man" has so far been the work of an aristocratic society — and so it will always be. Such a society believes in a long ladder of rank and worth among human beings, and it requires slavery in some form. Without the pathos of distance — the distance that grows from an embodied difference of classes, from the ruling caste's habit of looking out and down upon its subordinates and instruments, from its constant practice of obeying and commanding, of holding down and holding apart — that other, more mysterious pathos could never have arisen: the longing for an ever-greater widening of distance within the soul itself, the formation of ever higher, rarer, further, more extended, more comprehensive states — in short, the elevation of the type "man," the continued self-overcoming of man, to use a moral formula in a supermoral sense. One must not indulge any humanitarian illusions about the origin of an aristocratic society — that is, the precondition for the elevation of the type "man." The truth is hard. Let us acknowledge without prejudice how every higher civilization has hitherto originated! Men with a still natural nature, barbarians in every terrible sense of the word, men of prey, still possessed of unbroken strength of will and lust for power, flung themselves upon weaker, more moral, more peaceful races (perhaps trading or cattle-rearing communities), or upon old mellow civilizations in which the final vital force was flickering out in brilliant fireworks of wit and depravity. At the start, the noble caste was always the barbarian caste: their superiority lay not first of all in their physical but in their psychical power — they were more complete men (which at every point also means: more complete beasts).

before: 259. To refrain mutually from injury, violence, and exploitation, and to put one's will on a par with that of others — this can, in a certain rough sense, make for good conduct among individuals, provided the necessary conditions are present (that the individuals are actually similar in force and worth, and co-related within one organization). The moment one wishes to take this principle more generally, and possibly even as the fundamental principle of society, it at once reveals what it really is: a will to the denial of life, a principle of dissolution and decay. One must think here profoundly, to the very roots, and resist all sentimental weakness. Life itself is essentially appropriation, injury, conquest of the strange and weak, suppression, severity, the imposition of one's own forms, incorporation — at the very least and mildest: exploitation. But why should one forever use precisely these words, on which disparaging intent has long been stamped? Even that organization within which, as was previously supposed, individuals treat each other as equal — as happens in every healthy aristocracy — must itself, if it is a living and not a dying organization, do toward other bodies all that its members refrain from doing to one another. It will have to be an embodied will to power; it will seek to grow, to gain ground, to attract to itself and win ascendancy — not out of any morality or immorality, but because it lives, and because life is precisely will to power. On no point is the ordinary consciousness of Europeans more unwilling to be corrected than on this. People rave everywhere, even under the banner of science, about future conditions of society in which "the exploiting character" will be absent. To my ears that sounds as if they promised to invent a mode of life that dispensed with all organic functions. Exploitation does not belong to a depraved or primitive society; it belongs to the nature of the living being as a primary organic function. It is a consequence of the intrinsic will to power, which is precisely the will to life. As a theory this may be a novelty — as a reality it is the fundamental fact of all history. Let us be at least this honest with ourselves!

before: 260. On a journey through the many finer and coarser moralities that have prevailed or still prevail on earth, I found certain traits recurring together and linked with one another, until at last two primary types emerged and a fundamental distinction came to light. There is master-morality and slave-morality. I should add at once that in all higher and mixed civilizations there are also attempts at reconciling the two — more often still their confusion and mutual misunderstanding, and sometimes their close juxtaposition, even within the same man, within one soul. The distinctions of moral values have originated either in a ruling caste, pleasantly conscious of being different from those it ruled, or among the ruled — the slaves and dependents of every kind. In the first case, when it is the rulers who determine the concept "good," it is the exalted, proud states of soul that are felt to be what distinguishes and determines rank. The noble type of man separates from himself those in whom the opposite of such states shows itself; he despises them. It should be noted that in this first kind of morality the opposition "good" and "bad" means practically the same as "noble" and "despicable." The opposition "good" and "evil" has a different origin. The cowardly, the timid, the petty, those who think only of narrow utility are despised; so too the distrustful with their constrained glances, the self-abasing, the dog-like men who let themselves be mistreated, the mendicant flatterers, and above all the liars. It is a fundamental belief of all aristocrats that the common people are untruthful. "We truthful ones" — so the nobility called itself in ancient Greece. It is obvious that moral designations were first applied to men and only derivatively, at a later period, to actions. Historians of morals therefore make a gross mistake when they start with questions like "Why have sympathetic actions been praised?" The noble type of man feels himself to be the determiner of values. He does not require approval; he passes judgment: "What harms me is harmful in itself." He knows that it is he alone who confers honor on things; he is a creator of values. He honors whatever he recognizes in himself: such morality is self-glorification. In the foreground is the feeling of fullness, of power that seeks to overflow, the happiness of high tension, the consciousness of a wealth that would gladly give and bestow. The noble man also helps the unfortunate, but not — or scarcely — out of pity; rather from an impulse generated by the superabundance of power. The noble man honors in himself the powerful one, the man who has power over himself, who knows how to speak and how to keep silent, who takes pleasure in subjecting himself to severity and hardness, and who has reverence for all that is severe and hard. "Wotan placed a hard heart in my breast," an old Scandinavian saga says — rightly expressed from the soul of a proud Viking. Such a man is even proud of not being made for sympathy, and so the saga hero adds a warning: "He who has not a hard heart when young will never have one." The noble and brave who think in this way are the furthest removed from a morality that sees the characteristic of the moral precisely in sympathy, in acting for others, in désintéressement. Faith in oneself, pride in oneself, a fundamental enmity and irony toward "selflessness" — these belong as surely to noble morality as do a careless scorn and caution in the presence of sympathy and the "warm heart." It is the powerful who know how to honor; it is their art, their realm of invention. Profound reverence for age and tradition — all law rests on this double reverence — the belief and prejudice in favor of ancestors and against newcomers, is typical of the morality of the powerful. If, conversely, men of "modern ideas" believe almost instinctively in "progress" and "the future," and show less and less respect for age, the ignoble origin of these "ideas" has complacently betrayed itself. A morality of the ruling class is, however, most foreign and irritating to present-day taste in the sternness of its principle that one has duties only to one's equals; that toward beings of lower rank, toward all that is foreign, one may act as one pleases, or "as the heart desires," and in any case "beyond good and evil" — here sympathy and similar sentiments can find their place. The ability and duty to exercise prolonged gratitude and prolonged revenge — both only within the circle of equals — artfulness in retaliation, raffinement of the idea of friendship, a certain need for enemies (as outlets for the emotions of envy, quarrelsomeness, arrogance — in order, in fact, to be a good friend): all these are typical features of noble morality. As noted, it is not the morality of "modern ideas," and is therefore hard to realize today, and also hard to unearth and uncover. It is otherwise with the second type of morality, slave-morality. Suppose that the abused, the oppressed, the suffering, the unfree, the weary, and those uncertain of themselves moralize — what will be the common element in their moral estimates? A pessimistic suspicion about the entire human situation will probably find expression, perhaps a condemnation of man together with his situation. The slave has an unfavorable eye for the virtues of the powerful; he has a skepticism and distrust, a refinement of distrust for everything "good" that is honored there — he would like to persuade himself that even their happiness is not genuine. On the other hand, those qualities that serve to ease the existence of sufferers are brought forward and bathed in light: here sympathy, the kind and helping hand, the warm heart, patience, diligence, humility, and friendliness come to honor, for here these are the most useful qualities and almost the only means of bearing the burden of existence. Slave-morality is essentially a morality of utility. Here is the origin of the famous opposition "good" and "evil": power and dangerousness are assumed to reside in the evil — a certain dreadfulness, subtlety, and strength that do not allow themselves to be despised. According to slave-morality, then, the "evil" man arouses fear; according to master-morality, it is precisely the "good" man who arouses and wishes to arouse fear, while the "bad" man is thought of as the despicable being. The contrast reaches its peak when, in consistency with slave-morality, a shade of disparagement — it may be slight and well-meaning — attaches itself at last to the "good" man of this morality. On the servile mode of thought, the good man must in any case be the safe man: good-natured, easily deceived, perhaps a little stupid, un bonhomme. On a journey through the many finer and coarser moralities that have prevailed or still prevail on earth, I found certain traits recurring together and linked with one another, until at last two primary types emerged and a fundamental distinction came to light. There is master-morality and slave-morality. I should add at once that in all higher and mixed civilizations there are also attempts at reconciling the two — more often still their confusion and mutual misunderstanding, and sometimes their close juxtaposition, even within the same man, within one soul. The distinctions of moral values have originated either in a ruling caste, pleasantly conscious of being different from those it ruled, or among the ruled — the slaves and dependents of every kind. In the first case, when it is the rulers who determine the concept "good," it is the exalted, proud states of soul that are felt to be what distinguishes and determines rank. The noble type of man separates from himself those in whom the opposite of such states shows itself; he despises them. It should be noted that in this first kind of morality the opposition "good" and "bad" means practically the same as "noble" and "despicable." The opposition "good" and "evil" has a different origin. The cowardly, the timid, the petty, those who think only of narrow utility are despised; so too the distrustful with their constrained glances, the self-abasing, the dog-like men who let themselves be mistreated, the mendicant flatterers, and above all the liars. It is a fundamental belief of all aristocrats that the common people are untruthful. "We truthful ones" — so the nobility called itself in ancient Greece. It is obvious that moral designations were first applied to men and only derivatively, at a later period, to actions. The noble type of man feels himself to be the determiner of values. He does not require approval; he passes judgment: "What harms me is harmful in itself." He knows that it is he alone who confers honor on things; he is a creator of values. He honors whatever he recognizes in himself: such morality is self-glorification. In the foreground is the feeling of fullness, of power that seeks to overflow, the happiness of high tension, the consciousness of a wealth that would gladly give and bestow. The noble man also helps the unfortunate, but not — or scarcely — out of pity; rather from an impulse generated by the superabundance of power. The noble man honors in himself the powerful one, the man who has power over himself, who knows how to speak and how to keep silent, who takes pleasure in subjecting himself to severity and hardness, and who has reverence for all that is severe and hard. "Wotan placed a hard heart in my breast," an old Scandinavian saga says — rightly expressed from the soul of a proud Viking. Faith in oneself, pride in oneself, a fundamental enmity and irony toward "selflessness" — these belong as surely to noble morality as do a slight disdain and caution in the presence of sympathy and the "warm heart." It is the powerful who know how to honor; it is their art, their realm of invention. Profound reverence for age and tradition — all law rests on this double reverence — the belief and prejudice in favor of ancestors and against those to come, is typical of the morality of the powerful. If, conversely, men of "modern ideas" believe almost instinctively in "progress" and "the future," and show less and less respect for age, the ignoble origin of these "ideas" has already revealed itself clearly enough. before: 262. A species originates, and a type becomes established and strong, through the long struggle with essentially constant unfavorable conditions. On the other hand, breeders know by experience that species receiving superabundant nourishment, and in general a surplus of protection and care, immediately tend to develop variations strongly marked, and become fertile in prodigies and monstrosities (including monstrous vices). Now look at an aristocratic commonwealth — say, an ancient Greek polis or Venice — as a voluntary or involuntary arrangement for the rearing of human beings. There are men side by side, thrown on their own resources, who want to make their kind prevail, chiefly because they must prevail — or else face the terrible danger of extermination. The favor, the superabundance, the protection under which variations are fostered are lacking; the species needs itself as species, as something that, precisely through its hardness, its uniformity, and simplicity of structure, can prevail and make itself permanent in constant struggle with neighbors or with rebellious or rebellion-threatening vassals. The most varied experience teaches it what qualities have allowed it to exist despite all gods and men and have so far made it victorious: these qualities it calls virtues, and these alone it cultivates to maturity. It does so with severity — indeed it desires severity. Every aristocratic morality is intolerant in the education of youth, in the control of women, in marriage customs, in the relations of old and young, in penal laws (which have an eye only for the degenerate); it even counts intolerance among the virtues, under the name of "justice." A type with few but strongly marked features, a species of severe, warlike, shrewdly silent, reserved, and reticent men (who, precisely as such, have the most delicate sensibility for the charm and nuances of society), is thus established, unaffected by the vicissitudes of generations. The constant struggle with uniformly unfavorable conditions is, as noted, the cause of a type becoming stable and hard. Finally, however, a happy state comes: the enormous tension relaxes; perhaps there are no more enemies among neighboring peoples, and the means of life — even of the enjoyment of life — are present in superabundance. At one stroke the bond and constraint of the old discipline is severed: it is no longer felt necessary, no longer a condition of existence — if it is to continue, it can only do so as a form of luxury, as an archaizing taste. Variations, whether they be deviations (into the higher, finer, and rarer) or deteriorations and monstrosities, now appear suddenly on the scene in the greatest exuberance and splendor. The individual dares to be individual and to detach himself. At this turning point of history there appear, side by side and often mixed and entangled together, a magnificent, virgin-forest-like upward growth and upward striving, a kind of tropical tempo in the rivalry of growth, and an extraordinary decay and self-destruction, owing to the savagely opposing and seemingly exploding egoisms that strive against one another "for sun and light" and can no longer assign themselves any limit, restraint, or forbearance through the existing morality. It was this morality itself that piled up the strength so enormously, that bent the bow in so threatening a manner; it is now "out of date," it is getting "out of date." The dangerous and disquieting point has been reached when the greater, more manifold, more comprehensive life is lived beyond the old morality. The "individual" stands out and is obliged to have recourse to his own lawgiving, his own arts and artifices, for self-preservation, self-elevation, and self-deliverance. Nothing but new "Whys," nothing but new "Hows," no common formulas any longer; misunderstanding and disregard leagued together; decay, deterioration, and the loftiest desires frightfully entangled; the genius of the race overflowing from all the cornucopias of good and bad; a portentous simultaneity of spring and autumn, full of new charms and mysteries peculiar to the fresh, still inexhausted, still unwearied corruption. Danger is again present — the mother of morality — great danger, this time shifted into the individual, into neighbor and friend, into the street, into one's own child, into one's own heart, into all the most personal and secret recesses of desire and will. What will the moral philosophers of this time have to preach? They discover, these sharp observers and loafers, that the end is quickly approaching, that everything around them decays and produces decay, that nothing will last until the day after tomorrow — except one species of man, the incurably mediocre. The mediocre alone have a prospect of continuing and propagating themselves; they will be the men of the future, the sole survivors. "Be like them! Become mediocre!" is now the only morality that still has significance, that still gets a hearing. But it is difficult to preach this morality of mediocrity! It can never admit what it is and what it wants! It has to speak of moderation and dignity and duty and brotherly love — it will have trouble concealing its irony!

before: 264. It cannot be effaced from a man's soul what his ancestors most preferably and constantly did: whether they were perhaps diligent economizers attached to a desk and a cash-box, modest and citizen-like in their desires and in their virtues; or whether they were accustomed to commanding from morning till night, fond of rough pleasures and probably of rougher duties and responsibilities; or whether, finally, at some time they sacrificed old privileges of birth and possession in order to live wholly for their faith — for their "God" — as men of an inexorable and sensitive conscience that blushes at every compromise. It is quite impossible for a man not to have the qualities and predilections of his parents and ancestors in his constitution, whatever appearances may suggest to the contrary. This is the problem of race. Given that one knows something of the parents, one may draw a conclusion about the child: any kind of offensive incontinence, any kind of sordid envy, any kind of clumsy self-vaunting — the three things which together have constituted the genuine plebeian type in all times — must pass to the child as surely as bad blood; and with the help of the best education and culture one will only succeed in deceiving about such heredity. And what else does education and culture try to do nowadays! In our very democratic — or rather, very plebeian — age, "education" and "culture" must be essentially the art of deceiving: deceiving about origin, about the inherited plebeianism in body and soul. An educator who today preached truthfulness above everything else and constantly called out to his pupils, "Be true! Be natural! Show yourselves as you are!" — even such a virtuous and sincere ass would soon learn to resort to Horace's furca — naturam expellere — and with what results? Plebeianism usque recurret. [Footnote: Horace's "Epistles," I. x. 24.]

before: 265. At the risk of displeasing innocent ears, I submit that egoism belongs to the essence of a noble soul — I mean the unalterable belief that to a being such as "we," other beings must naturally be in subjection and must sacrifice themselves. The noble soul accepts the fact of his egoism without question, and also without any feeling of harshness, constraint, or arbitrariness, but rather as something that may have its basis in the primary law of things. If he sought a name for it, he would say: "It is justice itself." He acknowledges under certain circumstances, though they made him hesitate at first, that there are other equally privileged ones. As soon as he has settled this question of rank, he moves among these equals with the same assurance of modesty and delicate respect as he enjoys in dealing with himself — in accordance with an innate heavenly mechanism that all the stars understand. This artfulness and self-limitation in intercourse with his equals is another instance of his egoism: every star is a similar egoist. He honors himself in them, and in the rights he concedes to them; he has no doubt that the exchange of honors and rights, as the essence of all intercourse, belongs also to the natural condition of things. The noble soul gives as he takes, prompted by the passionate and sensitive instinct of requital that is at the root of his nature. The notion of "favor," inter pares, has neither significance nor good repute; there may be a sublime way of letting gifts, as it were, light upon one from above, and of drinking them thirstily like dew-drops, but the noble soul has no aptitude for those arts and displays. His egoism prevents it: in general he looks "aloft" unwillingly — he looks either forward, horizontally and deliberately, or downward: he knows that he is on a height.

before: 269. The more a psychologist — a born, an unavoidable psychologist and soul-diviner — turns his attention to the more select cases and individuals, the greater is his danger of being suffocated by sympathy. He needs sternness and cheerfulness more than any other man. For the corruption and ruination of higher men, of the more unusually constituted souls, is in fact the rule: it is dreadful to have such a rule always before one's eyes. The manifold torment of the psychologist who has discovered this ruination, who discovers it once and then discovers it almost repeatedly throughout all history — this universal inner "desperateness" of higher men, this eternal "too late!" in every sense — may perhaps one day cause him to turn with bitterness against his own lot and to attempt self-destruction: to "go to ruin" himself. In almost every psychologist one may perceive a telltale inclination for delightful intercourse with commonplace and well-ordered men; the fact is thereby disclosed that he always requires healing, that he needs a sort of flight and forgetfulness, away from what his insight and incisiveness — his "business" — has laid upon his conscience. The fear of his memory is peculiar to him. He is easily silenced by the judgment of others; he hears with unmoved countenance how people honor, admire, love, and glorify where he has perceived, or he even conceals his silence by expressly assenting to some plausible opinion. Perhaps the paradox of his situation becomes so dreadful that precisely where he has learned great sympathy together with great contempt, the multitude, the educated, and the visionaries have on their part learned great reverence — reverence for "great men" and marvelous animals for whose sake one blesses and honors the fatherland, the earth, the dignity of mankind, and oneself, to whom one points the young, and in view of whom one educates them. And who knows but in all great instances hitherto the same happened: that the multitude worshipped a god, and that the "god" was only a poor sacrificial animal! Success has always been the greatest liar — and the "work" itself is a success. The great statesman, the conqueror, the discoverer, are disguised in their creations until they are unrecognizable. The "work" of the artist or philosopher invents only the man who is credited with having created it; the "great men," as they are reverenced, are poor little fictions composed afterward. In the world of historical values, spurious coinage prevails. Those great poets — Byron, Musset, Poe, Leopardi, Kleist, Gogol (I do not venture to mention much greater names, but I have them in mind) — as they now appear, and perhaps had to be: men of the moment, enthusiastic, sensuous, and childish, light-minded and impulsive in their trust and distrust; with souls in which some flaw usually has to be concealed; often taking revenge with their works for an inner defilement, often seeking forgetfulness in their soaring from a too-true memory, often lost in the mud and almost in love with it, until they become like the will-o'-the-wisps around the swamps and pretend to be stars — the people then call them idealists — often struggling with protracted disgust, with an ever-reappearing phantom of disbelief that makes them cold and obliges them to languish for gloria and devour "faith as it is" from the hands of intoxicated adulators: what a torment these great artists and so-called higher men are to one who has once found them out! It is thus conceivable that it is just from woman — who is clairvoyant in the world of suffering, and also unfortunately eager to help and save far beyond her powers — that they have so readily learned those outbreaks of boundless devoted sympathy, which the multitude, especially the reverent multitude, do not understand, and which they overwhelm with prying and self-gratifying interpretations. This sympathizing invariably deceives itself as to its power; woman would like to believe that love can do everything — it is the superstition peculiar to her. Alas, he who knows the heart finds out how poor, helpless, pretentious, and blundering even the best and deepest love is — that it rather destroys than saves! It is possible that under the holy fable and travesty of the life of Jesus there is hidden one of the most painful cases of the martyrdom of knowledge about love: the martyrdom of the most innocent and most craving heart, one that never had enough of any human love, that demanded love, that demanded inexorably and frantically to be loved and nothing else, with terrible outbursts against those who refused him their love; the story of a poor soul insatiated and insatiable in love, that had to invent hell to send there those who would not love him — and that at last, enlightened about human love, had to invent a God who is entire love, entire capacity for love — who takes pity on human love, because it is so paltry, so ignorant! He who has such sentiments, he who has such knowledge about love — seeks death! But why dwell on such painful matters? Unless, of course, one is obliged to.

before: 293. A man who says: "I like that, I take it for my own, and mean to guard and protect it from every one"; a man who can conduct a case, carry out a resolution, remain true to an opinion, keep hold of a woman, punish and overthrow insolence; a man who has his indignation and his sword, and to whom the weak, the suffering, the oppressed — and even the animals — willingly submit and naturally belong; in short, a man who is a master by nature — when such a man has sympathy, well! That sympathy has value! But of what account is the sympathy of those who suffer! Or of those who even preach sympathy! There is nowadays, throughout almost the whole of Europe, a sickly irritability and sensitiveness toward pain, and also a repulsive unrestrainedness in complaining, an effeminization that, with the aid of religion and philosophical nonsense, seeks to dress itself up as something superior — there is a regular cult of suffering. The unmanliness of what is called "sympathy" by such groups of visionaries is always, I believe, the first thing that strikes the eye. One must resolutely and radically taboo this latest form of bad taste; and finally I wish people to put the good amulet, gai saber ("gay science," in ordinary language), on heart and neck, as a protection against it.

before: 294. The Olympian vice. — Despite the philosopher who, as a genuine Englishman, tried to bring laughter into bad repute in all thinking minds — "Laughing is a bad infirmity of human nature, which every thinking mind will strive to overcome" (Hobbes) — I would even allow myself to rank philosophers according to the quality of their laughing — up to those who are capable of golden laughter. And supposing that gods also philosophize, which I am strongly inclined to believe, owing to many reasons — I have no doubt that they also know how to laugh thereby in an overman-like and new fashion — and at the expense of all serious things! Gods are fond of ridicule: it seems that they cannot refrain from laughter even in holy matters.

before: 295. The genius of the heart, as that great mysterious one possesses it — the tempter-god and born rat-catcher of consciences, whose voice can descend into the nether-world of every soul; who neither speaks a word nor casts a glance in which there is not some motive or touch of allurement; to whose perfection it pertains that he knows how to appear — not as he is, but in a guise that acts as an additional constraint on his followers to press ever closer to him, to follow him more cordially and thoroughly; the genius of the heart, which imposes silence and attention on everything loud and self-conceited, which smooths rough souls and makes them taste a new longing — to lie placid as a mirror, that the deep heavens may be reflected in them; the genius of the heart, which teaches the clumsy and too-hasty hand to hesitate, and to grasp more delicately; which scents the hidden and forgotten treasure, the drop of goodness and sweet spirituality under thick dark ice, and is a divining-rod for every grain of gold long buried and imprisoned in mud and sand; the genius of the heart, from contact with which everyone goes away richer — not favored or surprised, not as though gratified and oppressed by the good things of others, but richer in himself, newer than before, broken up, blown upon, and sounded by a thawing wind; more uncertain perhaps, more delicate, more fragile, more bruised, but full of hopes which as yet lack names, full of a new will and current, full of a new ill-will and counter-current… But what am I doing, my friends? Of whom am I talking to you? Have I forgotten myself so far that I have not even told you his name? Unless you have already divined of your own accord who this questionable god and spirit is, that wishes to be praised in such a manner? For, as it happens to everyone who from childhood onward has always been on his legs, and in foreign lands, I have also encountered on my path many strange and dangerous spirits; above all, however, and again and again, the one of whom I have just spoken: in fact, no less a personage than the god Dionysus, the great equivocator and tempter, to whom, as you know, I once offered in all secrecy and reverence my first-fruits — the last, as it seems to me, who has offered a sacrifice to him, for I have found no one who could understand what I was then doing. In the meantime, however, I have learned much, far too much, about the philosophy of this god, and, as I said, from mouth to mouth — I, the last disciple and initiate of the god Dionysus: and perhaps I might at last begin to give you, my friends, as far as I am allowed, a little taste of this philosophy? In a hushed voice, as is but seemly: for it has to do with much that is secret, new, strange, wonderful, and uncanny. The very fact that Dionysus is a philosopher, and that therefore gods also philosophize, seems to me a novelty which is not unensnaring, and which might perhaps arouse suspicion precisely among philosophers — among you, my friends, there is less to be said against it, except that it comes too late and not at the right time; for, as has been disclosed to me, you are loath nowadays to believe in God and gods. It may happen, too, that in the frankness of my story I must go further than is agreeable to the strict usages of your ears. Certainly the god in question went further, very much further, in such dialogues, and was always many paces ahead of me… Indeed, if it were allowed, I should have to give him, according to human usage, fine ceremonious titles of lustre and merit; I should have to extol his courage as investigator and discoverer, his fearless honesty, truthfulness, and love of wisdom. But such a god does not know what to do with all that respectable trumpery and pomp. "Keep that," he would say, "for thyself and those like thee, and whoever else requires it! I — have no reason to cover my nakedness!" One suspects that this kind of divinity and philosopher perhaps lacks shame. He once said: "Under certain circumstances I love mankind" — and referred thereby to Ariadne, who was present — "in my opinion man is an agreeable, brave, inventive animal, that has not his equal upon earth; he makes his way even through all labyrinths. I like man, and often think how I can still further advance him, and make him stronger, more evil, and more profound." — "Stronger, more evil, and more profound?" I asked in horror. "Yes," he said again, "stronger, more evil, and more profound; also more beautiful" — and thereby the tempter-god smiled with his halcyon smile, as though he had just paid some charming compliment. One here sees at once that it is not only shame that this divinity lacks; and in general there are good grounds for supposing that in some things the gods could all of them come to us men for instruction. We men are — more human.

before: 296. Alas! what are you, after all, my written and painted thoughts! Not long ago you were so variegated, young, and malicious, so full of thorns and secret spices, that you made me sneeze and laugh — and now? You have already doffed your novelty, and some of you, I fear, are ready to become truths, so immortal do they look, so pathetically honest, so tedious! And was it ever otherwise? What then do we write and paint, we mandarins with Chinese brush, we immortalizers of things that lend themselves to writing — what are we alone capable of painting? Alas, only that which is just about to fade and begins to lose its odor! Alas, only exhausted and departing storms and belated yellow sentiments! Alas, only birds strayed and fatigued by flight, which now let themselves be captured with the hand — with our hand! We immortalize what cannot live and fly much longer — things only which are exhausted and mellow! And it is only for your afternoon, you, my written and painted thoughts, for which alone I have colors, many colors perhaps, many variegated softenings, and fifty yellows and browns and greens and reds — but nobody will divine thereby how you looked in your morning, you sudden sparks and marvels of my solitude, you, my old, beloved — evil thoughts!

We immortalize what cannot live and fly much longer — things only which are exhausted and mellow! And it is only for your afternoon, you, my written and painted thoughts, for which alone I have colors, many colors perhaps, many brightly coloured caresses, and fifty yellows and browns and greens and reds — but nobody will divine thereby how you looked in your morning, you sudden sparks and marvels of my solitude, you, my old, beloved — evil thoughts!
reason: Zärtlichkeiten means caresses/tenderness, not softenings.

before:
Midday of life! O season of delight!
My summer's park!
A restless joy to look, to wait, to hark —
I watch for friends, ready day and night —
Where do you linger, friends? The time is right!
after:
O midday of life! Solemn hour!
O summer garden!
Restless joy in standing, watching, waiting—
I wait for friends, ready day and night.
Where are you, friends? Come! It is time! It is time!
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Restore solemn time, watching/waiting and repeated call; no delight/hark rhyme.

before:
Is not the glacier's grey today, for you,
Rose-garlanded?
The brook seeks you; wind and cloud, with longing thread,
Thrust themselves higher toward the blue,
To spy you from the eagle's farthest view.
after:
Was it not for you that the glacier’s grey
decks itself with roses today?
The brook seeks you; wind and cloud press on,
longing, higher into the blue today,
to spy you from the farthest bird’s-eye view.
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Restore bird viewpoint not a specified eagle and wind/cloud without invented thread.

before:
My table was spread out for you on high —
Who dwells up here,
Star-near, so near the grisly pit below?
My realm — what realm has wider boundary?
My honey — who has sipped its fragrancy?
after:
On the heights my table was laid for you.
Who lives so near
the stars, so near the abyss’s dread expanses?
My realm—what realm has reached out farther?
And my honey—who has tasted it? ...
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Restore abyss distances and honey tasted rather than fragrance sipped.

before:
Friends, you are there! Alas — yet I am not
The one you seek?
You stare and stop — better your wrath should speak!
Am I not I? Hand, gait, face — changed? And what
I am, to you my friends, now am I not?
after:
There you ARE, friends! Alas, am I not the one
you meant to find?
You hesitate, you marvel—ah, I’d rather you were angry!
Am I no longer he? Hand, step, face—all changed?
And WHAT I am, am I not that to you, my friends?
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Restore questions and opposition between speaker and friends.

before:
Have I become another? Strange to Me?
Yet sprung from Me?
A wrestler who too often wrings himself?
Too often thwarting my own soul's full reach,
Wounded and hampered by my own self-victory?
after:
Have I become another? A stranger to myself?
Escaped from my own self?
A wrestler who too often overcame himself?
Too often braced against my own strength,
wounded and hampered by my own victory?
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Self-overcoming and wounds rather than wringing or limiting soul’s reach.

before:
I sought where the wind blows keenest. There
I learned to dwell
Where no man dwells, on lonesome ice-lost fell,
And unlearned man and god and curse and prayer —
Became a ghost that haunts the glaciers bare?
after:
Did I seek the place where the wind blows keenest?
Did I learn to live
where no one lives, in barren polar-bear country,
unlearn man and god, curse and prayer?
Become a ghost that walks on glaciers?
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Restore polar-bear regions, full questioning structure and unlearning.

before:
You, my old friends! Look! You turn pale, filled through
With love and fear!
Go! But not in anger. You could never live here.
Here in the farthest realm of ice and scree
One must be a huntsman — must leap like chamois, free.
after:
My old friends! Look! How pale you look,
full of love and dread!
No, go! Do not be angry. YOU could not live here,
here in the farthest realm of ice and rock:
one must be a hunter here, and like a chamois.
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Restore mountains/goat likeness; no invented freedom.

before:
An evil huntsman — was I? See how taut
My bow was bent!
Strongest was he by whom such shaft was sent —
Yet woe! That arrow is with peril fraught,
Perilous as none. — Seek the safe homes you sought!
after:
A DANGEROUS hunter I have become! See how steeply
my bow is drawn!
The strongest was the one who made such a draw.
But woe now! Dangerous is THAT arrow
as NO other is—away from here, for your own sake! ...
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Speaker became a hunter, bow is drawn, no invented safe homes.

before:
You go! You have endured enough, O heart —
Strong was your hope;
To new friends open wide your gates, your scope,
Let old ones be. Bid memory depart!
Were you young then? — now, better young you art!
after:
You turn away? O heart, you have borne enough.
Your hope stayed strong.
Keep your doors open for NEW friends!
Let the old go! Let the memory go!
If you were young once, you are better young now!
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Singular heart addressed; no invented scope.

before:
What once linked us together, one hope's tie —
(Who now could trace
those lines, now fading, Love once wrote thereon?) —
Is like a parchment that the hand shies by
To touch — like crackling leaves, all seared, all dry.
after:
What once bound us, the bond of one hope—
who still reads the signs,
the pale signs love once wrote into it?
I liken it to parchment the hand
SHRINKS from grasping—like it, browned and burned.
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Restore inscribed band/hand-shy parchment, no invented crackling leaves.

before:
Oh! Friends no more! They are — what name for those? —
Friends' phantom-flight
Knocking at my heart's window-pane at night,
Gazing at me, that speaks "We were" — and goes. —
O withered words, once fragrant as the rose!
after:
Friends no longer—what shall I call them?
Only ghosts of friends!
Even now it knocks at my heart and window at night,
looks at me and says, ‘Yet we WERE your friends?’
O withered word that once smelled of roses!
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Heart and window are distinct; ghost-friends not phantom flight.

before:
Yearnings of youth that could not understand!
For whom I pined,
Whom I believed were changed with me, my kind:
But they grew old, and thus were doomed and banned —
None but new kin are native of my land!
after:
O longing of youth that misunderstood itself!
Those I longed for,
whom I thought changed with me and kin to me—
their growing OLD has banished them.
Only those who change remain my kin.
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Restore changing to remain kin; old version invented new kin in native land.

before:
Midday of life! My second youth's delight!
My summer's park!
A restless joy to long, to wait, to hark!
I watch for friends! — ready day and night,
For my new friends. Come! Come! The time is right!
after:
O midday of life! My second youth!
O summer garden!
Restless joy in standing, watching, waiting!
I wait for friends, ready day and night,
for NEW friends! Come! It is time! It is time!
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Restore repeated standing/watching/waiting and doubled time.

after:
THIS song is over—the sweet cry of longing
died on my lips.
A sorcerer did it, the friend at the right hour,
the midday friend—no, do not ask who it was.
It was at midday that one became two ...
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Longing not remorse/rue; cry dies in mouth; one becomes two.

before:
We keep our Feast of Feasts, sure of our bourne,
Our aims the same:
The Guest of Guests, friend Zarathustra, came!
The world now laughs, the grisly veil is torn,
And Light and Dark were one that wedding-morn.
after:
Now, certain of our common victory, we celebrate
the feast of feasts:
friend ZARATHUSTRA came, the guest of guests!
Now the world laughs; the dreadful curtain tore.
The wedding came for light and darkness ...
reason: New close five-line stanza from German: Restore shared victory not destination, and wedding of light/dark without invented wedding morning or fusion.
